one_liner: Header PRNGs from an x86 test bench: 3-round AES counter and carry-less-multiply generators, about 4x std::mt19937 per call.
what_it_does: prng-test-bench is a Google Benchmark plus PractRand harness for about 80 generators. Two of its own headers, include/aes_ctr_128.hpp (returns __uint128_t) and include/clmulrand.hpp (returns uint64_t), are the catalogued items. Each generator is a small struct that satisfies std::uniform_random_bit_generator (static_assert in urbg_base_class.hpp), so it plugs into std distributions and std::shuffle. Construction is by default ctor (seeded from arc4random_buf), a raw state value, or a std::array of seed bytes; it is not a full RandomNumberEngine.
how_it_is_fast: Both are counter-based: the state is a pair of 64-bit Weyl counters advanced with one _mm_add_epi64 per call, so there is no long dependency chain like the 624-word Mersenne Twister state. aes_ctr_128 mixes the counter with three _mm_aesenc_si128 rounds under one per-generator key and returns all 128 bits. clmulrand does one PCLMULQDQ of the counter's two lanes against each other and returns the high minus the low 64-bit half. Both are a handful of instructions with no branches or table lookups.
when_to_use: Monte Carlo, simulation or randomized algorithms on x86-64 built with g++, where std::mt19937 or std::mt19937_64 shows up in profiles.
Callers that can consume 128 bits per call (two doubles, or two 64-bit draws) and want the most bits per call: aes_ctr_128 needs AES-NI.
64-bit draws one at a time with a 16-byte state: clmulrand needs PCLMULQDQ and SSE4.1.
One generator object per thread: the state is small (aes_ctr_128 32 bytes, clmulrand 16 bytes per the repo's prng-dump info table), so per-thread instances are cheap.
when_not_to_use: Anything that needs unpredictability (keys, tokens, nonces): aes_ctr_128 is 3 AES rounds with a fixed key on a Weyl counter, not AES-128-CTR, and clmulrand is a non-cryptographic mixer.
clang++ or MSVC builds (README: clang++ is not supported), or non-x86 targets: the headers use x86 intrinsics and compile only when __AES__ or __PCLMUL__ is defined.

Code that needs RandomNumberEngine features: seed(), discard/jump-ahead, operator==, stream I/O, or a fixed default-constructed sequence (urbg_base_class.hpp says it does not meet those requirements).
Platforms without arc4random_buf and explicit_bzero (the base class calls both: default seeding and zeroing in the destructor), e.g. older glibc or Windows.
Projects that want a packaged, versioned library: these are headers inside a test-bench repo with 2 stars, no releases and frequent commits.

integration.dependencies: none external; each header pulls sibling headers from include/ (urbg_base_class.hpp, wyprimes.hpp, plus mm_cast.hpp, simd_types.hpp and sha2_iv.h for aes_ctr_128, and clmum.hpp and mum.hpp for clmulrand); the benchmark itself needs Google Benchmark
integration.min_toolchain: g++ only; the Makefile builds with -std=c++26 (the base class uses C++20 concepts); the lowest working GCC version is not documented
integration.platforms: x86-64 little-endian (simd_types.hpp static_asserts it) with SSE4.1 plus AES-NI and __int128 (aes_ctr_128) or PCLMULQDQ (clmulrand); a libc that provides arc4random_buf and explicit_bzero (glibc 2.36+ or BSD)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; each object mutates its own state without synchronization, so use one instance per thread (as the benchmark does).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: usable wherever a std::uniform_random_bit_generator is accepted (std distributions, std::shuffle), but the seeding interface differs from std::mt19937 (no 32-bit seed or seed_seq constructor, no seed(), discard() or operator==), and aes_ctr_128's result_type is __uint128_t rather than a 32-bit value

gotchas: The benchmark's std::mt19937 baseline is skewed by type width. The repo's own prng-dump info table lists std::mt19937 (and std::philox4x32, minstd_rand) with a 64-bit result type (uint_fast32_t) and max 4294967295. So bytes_per_second credits mt19937 with 8 bytes per call, and prng-dump writes 32 zero bits per word into PractRand. Per call, aes_ctr_128 is about 4.0x and clmulrand about 4.5x std::mt19937 (derived from page data), not the 2.0x and 2.25x in the record. The 256 MB PractRand 'failures' of std::mt19937 and std::philox4x32 are harness artifacts, not properties of those engines.

Results/prng-next-benchmark.json shows that wyrand, clmulrand and aes_ctr_128 all take 0.38 to 0.48 ns real time per call, inside a loop that stores every result to a volatile. Their GiB/s ranking is mostly output width (128 vs 64 bits), not per-call speed (derived from page data).

aes_ctr_128 needs the key's two 64-bit lanes to differ: with equal lanes, swapping the counter lanes swaps the output lanes. init() has forced this (xor with SHA-512 IV words) only since the 2026-09-20 commits, two days after the published 2026-09-18 benchmark run; that change touches seeding, not next().
Copying a generator duplicates its stream (copy constructors are defaulted), and default construction makes a syscall-backed arc4random_buf call, so construct per thread or task, not per draw.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick aes_ctr_128 or clmulrand when you want a per-call std-compatible generator object on x86-64 with g++. lemire/testingRNG's aesctr and andanteyk's Culumi are the closest AES- and CLMUL-based relatives with their own timings. SHISHUA is the better fit when you fill large buffers in bulk. For unpredictable output use randp, an AES-CTR pool by the same author, not these.
verified_claims_summary: One author-run Google Benchmark pass (2026-09-18, 7 threads on an 8-vCPU VM named arch-vm, likely a Raptor Lake host; g++ -O3 -flto=auto -march=native; median of 5) gives per-thread GiB/s of 37.22 for aes_ctr_128, 21.03 for clmulrand, 4.67 for std::mt19937 and 5.24 for std::mt19937_64. Corrected for std::mt19937's 8-byte result type, that is about 2.50 and 2.82 billion calls/s against 0.63 billion: about 4.0x and 4.5x per call, about 3.5x and 4.0x against std::mt19937_64 (derived from page data). These are first-party numbers on an unnamed CPU.
status_note: Very actively maintained (743 commits; the last on 2026-10-02 is a formatting change) and MPL-2.0 per SPDX headers (there is no LICENSE file), so copying a header means keeping its MPL file-level notice; expect numbers to move between runs.
